title: The Catalogue That Told Climbers to Buy Fewer Chouinard Pitons
dek: In 1972 two climbers who made the best-known pitons in America used their first catalogue to ask customers to stop hammering them into the rock.

story.event: Scaling back the pitons that were their main product and promoting removable chocks in the 1972 catalogue
story.summary: By 1970 Chouinard Equipment, run by Yvon Chouinard and Tom Frost, was the largest supplier of climbing hardware in the United States, and its hard-steel pitons were scarring Yosemite's cracks. In their first catalogue, in 1972, the partners urged climbers to use removable aluminium chocks instead, printed Doug Robinson's essay on climbing without pitons, and scaled back the piton business; by the company's account, piton sales withered within months and chocks sold faster than they could be made.
paragraphs: In 1972 Chouinard Equipment mailed its first catalogue, and the essay that opened it asked customers to stop leaning on the product that had built the company. "Granite is delicate and soft," Yvon Chouinard and Tom Frost wrote, "much softer than the alloy steel pitons being hammered into it."

Pitons were where Chouinard had begun. In 1957 he bought a used coal-fired forge and an anvil from a junkyard, taught himself blacksmithing and started making hard steel pitons that could be removed and reused, selling them for $1.50 each. In the mid-1960s he went into business with Frost, an engineer and one of his Yosemite climbing partners. By 1970, Patagonia's company history says, Chouinard Equipment was the largest supplier of climbing hardware in the United States.

What the partners could see was damage done partly by their own products. On popular Yosemite routes each piton was hammered in and then hammered out again, and their catalogue described cracks "degenerating into series of piton holes" and flakes being broken off. In the early 1970s, Stanford Magazine later reported, Frost and Chouinard grew increasingly alarmed, although the pitons were crucial to their business. There was an alternative: aluminium chocks, wedged into cracks and removed again by hand. The catalogue pointed to England, where decades of climbing without pitons had left the protection cracks in mint condition.

The partners decided to shrink the piton business, a move the company's history later called a big risk. The 1972 catalogue still sold pitons, but it put chocks first, carried a 14-page essay by the Sierra climber Doug Robinson on climbing without them, and ended its opening with a request: "Employ restraint and good judgement in the use of Chouinard equipment."

By the company's account, within a few months of the mailing the piton business had withered and chocks were selling faster than they could be made. The catalogue is still described as a turning point in climbing's ethics. A few years later Frost and his wife, Dorene, sold their share to Chouinard and his wife, Malinda, as the clothing line that became Patagonia grew.

quote.text: At the same time that we are earnest to explore and learn all things, we require that all things be mysterious and unexplorable, that land and sea be infinitely wild, unsurveyed and unfathomed by us because unfathomable.
quote.source_title: Walden, and On The Duty Of Civil Disobedience, Project Gutenberg eBook #205
quote.connection: Thoreau names the double wish inside the 1972 catalogue: to climb everything and still have the rock stay wild. Chouinard Equipment went on selling the tools of exploration while asking customers to leave less trace, and its founders did not pretend that tension away.

reflection: It is rare to see a business write, in its own catalogue, that customers should use its main product less. Chouinard and Frost could do it because they had looked hard at what their pitons were doing to the walls they loved, and because something better was ready to offer.

You may have a habit or a way of working that once served you well and is now wearing something down, perhaps your evenings or your patience. It does not have to go all at once. The pitons were not abolished; they were put second.
invitation: Name one tool or habit you reach for by default, at work or at home. For today, try the gentler alternative once, and notice whether anything you needed was lost.

cross_checks.claim: Chouinard began forging reusable steel pitons in 1957 and sold them for $1.50 each
Pitons were central to Chouinard Equipment's business when the partners became alarmed at the damage they did to the rock
The first catalogue, in 1972, opened with Chouinard and Frost's clean-climbing essay urging climbers to use chocks instead of pitons
The decision scaled the piton business back rather than ending it: the 1972 catalogue still offered pitons

research_notes: Separate episode: this edition is about the 1972 move from pitons to chocks at Chouinard Equipment, not Patagonia's 1991 growth crisis and layoffs, which it does not mention; no Chouinard or Patagonia edition existed in offline/editions when it was written. The company field is 'Chouinard Equipment' (the hardware business), since Patagonia began as its clothing line. Scale of the change: Patagonia's history says the partners 'decided to minimize the piton business'; The New Yorker says they 'stopped making pitons'; the 1972 catalogue itself still described pitons such as the RURP (Alpinist) and recommended fixed pitons where necessary, so the story says they shrank the piton business and that the catalogue still sold pitons. Share of sales: a 37signals blog post and Wikipedia say pitons were 70 percent of the business or income, but Wikipedia's only citation (Fashion Planet, 1998) is dead and the blog gives no source, so the figure is not used; the story relies on Patagonia's 'largest supplier of climbing hardware' and Stanford Magazine's 'crucial to their business'. Outcome: 'within a few months the piton business had atrophied; chocks sold faster than they could be made' is the company's own account and is attributed to it. Partnership dates: Patagonia says Chouinard went into partnership with Frost in 1965; Chouinard's own Outside excerpt says Frost was his partner from 1966 to 1975; the story says 'the mid-1960s'. Catalogue wording is quoted from R. A. Hutchins's 2002 transcription on climbaz.com, checked against the passages quoted by Signal v. Noise and Stanford Magazine (Stanford gives 'other climbers' where the transcription has 'other climber'); the patagonia.com pages carrying the essay ('A Word') and the clean-climbing catalogue were showing a maintenance notice during research and are not cited. Thoreau's passage is about wildness around a village, applied by analogy to rock climbing.
